item.title: These Birds Are Louder Than Elephants, Jackhammers and Chain Saws
item.description:
Deep in the Serra do Mar mountains of Brazil, a curious call echoes from high in the jungle canopy. The sound is practically deafening, a loud metallic pang that cuts through the forest’s thick foliage.

The bare-throated bellbird, which produces such calls to attract female mates, is no larger than a dove. And yet his song is louder than a jackhammer or a chain saw. It’s louder than an elephant’s trumpet.

It is, according a new scientific study, one of the loudest birdsongs ever recorded.

“They can even exceed elephants and lions and wolves and bison,” said João Menezes, an evolutionary biologist and lead author of the study, recently published in the journal Evolution.

Joining the bellbird at the top of the volume charts, the researchers found, is another Brazilian species: the red-legged seriema.

The two birds now join a previously identified bellbird species as the loudest avians known to science.

The study also uncovered a few of the anatomical traits that allow these birds to belt such powerful songs, answering many of the questions underlying the mysteries of birdsong.

“This new study is by far the largest cross-species comparison of sound amplitude in birds,” said Gonçalo Cardoso, an ornithologist at the University of Porto who was not involved with the research. “This is just the tip of the iceberg.”

The new work focuses specifically on amplitude, a measure of the height of a sound wave, which helps determine how far a sound can travel. Amplitude is a major component of loudness and is crucial to our perception of sound.

“Until recently, it was very impractical to go out into the field and measure amplitude,” Dr. Menezes said.

To accurately measure amplitude, researchers have to be able to distinguish one bird from many and pinpoint its exact distance from where they are recording. Because of that difficulty, birdsong amplitudes have remained a black box for researchers. Even the Canada goose, one of the most well-known and easily identifiable bird species alive today, has not had its amplitude measured, according to Dr. Menezes. “It’s kind of stepping into a whole new world,” he said.

In the new work, Dr. Menezes and his colleagues used two tools to measure birdsong in the wild. One of them, a range finder, is the same laser device golfers use to measure the distance to holes on a course. The other instrument, a sound level meter, allows researchers to pinpoint whichever bird is making the call, isolating it from background noise and other birds.

The researchers began their work early in the Covid-19 pandemic, when lockdowns kept quiet streets in Amherst, Mass.

“It was just this wonderful time where you can walk outside unmolested, no trucks, no buses, and get beautiful, scintillatingly clear recordings,” said Jeff Podos, a behavioral ecologist and bird expert at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and a co-author of the study. The team then moved on to the Atlantic Forest, jungles and savannas of Brazil, where there is a much greater diversity of bird species.

In total, the researchers documented 123 birdsong amplitudes, creating a database they could plumb for insights about what enables the birds to sing such different songs.

They found that amplitude varied widely across species, with the softest songs coming from hummingbirds, whose tunes registered around 50 decibels — similar to the sound of moderate rainfall.

But the bare-throated bellbird and the red-legged seriema stood out from the crowd.

The bellbird lives in the Atlantic Forest of Brazil, while the seriema, which is about as tall as a crane, lives on the country’s savanna.

Bellbirds have a distinct metallic chirp, while seriemas sing elaborate, melancholic songs that have been the subject of poetry. Both birds produced tunes that registered between 121 and 122 decibels.

“The bellbirds are really super interesting,” Dr. Podos said, “because not only are they that loud, but they make those loud sounds with that small body size.”

Birds are capable of singing with such volume in part because they have a uniquely evolved organ called a syrinx, which takes air from the lungs and projects it through the long tube of the trachea.

“It’s like a tube which serves the same function that a tube on a musical instrument does, like a trombone or a trumpet,” Dr. Podos said. “It helps concentrate the energy into a narrow range of frequencies, so it’s easier to hit louder peaks.”

By comparing the birds’ anatomies with their calls, the researchers found two additional features that contribute to amplitude: beak width and overall bird size. Wide beaks act like the bells on the end of brass instruments, allowing the birds to project a broader sound. Bigger birds, Dr. Menezes said, are aided by hardier, stronger throats.

“Larger birds tend to have larger, bulkier muscles, which can create more internal air pressure,” he said. “And air pressure is exactly what generates loud sounds.”

item.title: Russians Snap Up Chinese E.V.s as Ukrainian Attacks Make Fuel Scarce
item.description:
Sergei Tselikov, Russia’s leading auto industry expert, has owned more than 20 vehicles, including a Volvo, a Volkswagen and a Range Rover. All had gasoline engines.

But in July, as Ukrainian drone strikes against oil refineries left drivers across the country waiting for hours at gas stations, he bought a fully electric Chinese hatchback. He had to act quickly — the price of the car, made by Great Wall Motor, went up by about $2,000 within days as demand surged.

“I tried to fill up one of my cars and drove around to five nearby gas stations, but they had only diesel or lower-grade petrol,” he said, referring to the poorer-quality fuels the government has allowed to be sold to address the shortages. “I was just too lazy to stand in line.”

As Ukraine increasingly takes the war to Russia, the effects may be most visible on the roads. Since the end of June, Russia’s electric-vehicle market has more than doubled. Most of the E.V.s sold in the country are Chinese, a testament to Moscow’s economic pivot in response to Western wartime sanctions.

Russia is playing catch-up. For years, while other nations built out E.V. supply chains and charging infrastructure, Russia looked the other way. Its position as one of the world’s top oil producers used to keep gasoline cheap. Vast distances between major cities meant charging networks were economically unviable without guaranteed demand. And harsh winters required automakers to heavily adapt models to the climate.

Now, E.V.s are suddenly a more common sight on Russian roads, particularly in major cities. The number of electric vehicles, including hybrids, sold in the country went from 43,000 in the January-to-August period of 2025 to more than 83,000 over the same period this year, according to the Russian Ministry of Industry and Trade.

By the end of September, the share of pure electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids that can run without gas had reached 11.5 percent of the Russian car market, up from about 5 percent at the beginning of the year, according to Avtostat, an auto research agency led by Mr. Tselikov. The E.V. market share in Russia is now slightly higher than in the United States, but it is only a small fraction of the share in China, which is 45 percent.

While the E.V. surge in Russia stems from a specific factor — Ukrainian attacks — the shift there is the latest example of how war and supply shocks can quickly transform car-buying decisions.

E.V. sales have boomed in other parts of the world because of the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran, which has caused oil and gasoline prices to soar. Globally, E.V.s are on track to account for a record 29 percent of all new car purchases this year, according to the International Energy Agency.

E.V. sales have risen in more than 90 countries this year, including Brazil, Australia, India and South Korea. The I.E.A. said the energy crisis had “clearly reinforced the case for E.V.s.”

In Russia, the fuel shortages are unnerving many Russians who had grown accustomed to the war in Ukraine being only a distant nuisance. They threaten to become a serious political issue for the government.

On Friday, only 46 percent of gas stations across Russia were selling fuel, according to Gdebenz, a crowdsourced tool that tracks the fuel market. In Moscow, gasoline was available at 53 percent of stations, leading to some lines. In Nizhny Novgorod, a major city east of Moscow, the figure was only 27 percent.

The situation in Moscow was worse in early July and mid-August, when only a quarter of stations had fuel after strikes on refineries that supply the city.

At the time, gasoline lines clogged traffic across the capital. Drivers waited hours for gas at stations on the highways connecting Moscow with St. Petersburg, Kazan and the country’s south. President Vladimir V. Putin had opened these roads with great pride over the past decade.

To try to quell the crisis, the government permitted the sale of lower-grade gasoline and diesel. But some cars began to break down after using the lower-quality fuel.

Aleksandr, the manager of a Moscow repair shop specializing in Volvos, said that within two weeks in August, he had received 15 vehicles with clogged diesel soot filters, a problem he attributed to lower-grade fuel. He, like others interviewed for this article, asked that his last name not be used to avoid any trouble with the authorities.

As the fuel crisis has continued, E.V. dealerships have been cleared out, and online listings for used electric cars have dwindled.

At a sprawling dealership complex northwest of Moscow, a manager at Evolute, a brand of Russian-assembled electric vehicles based on Chinese designs, said there was no inventory left on the lot and no way to join a waiting list.

The complex houses more than 40 dealerships, most of which used to sell primarily brands from the West, Japan and South Korea. It now has more than 25 Chinese showrooms.

Many Russian car factories used to produce Western brands but were abandoned after the invasion of Ukraine under pressure from Western governments. Most now assemble Chinese cars.

On Moscow’s streets and in its parking lots, lines have appeared at charging stations, albeit shorter ones.

Aleksandr, 40, was charging a red Moskvich, an iconic Soviet brand revived using a rebadged Chinese design, one recent day. He said he had to drive around central Moscow to find a working charger with no line.

“Overall, the infrastructure is lacking,” Aleksandr said. The Moskvich belonged to his employer, he said, adding that he would never buy an E.V. for himself because of the expense and the lack of charging stations.

Some residents have turned to electric bikes or scooters, or tried to convert their cars to using natural gas. Others have switched to public transit, including intercity buses.

The gasoline shortage has become such a feature of daily life that even clowns at Moscow’s circus have cracked jokes about it. (“Does anyone have car keys? No? Well, of course not — there’s no gas!”)

The shift toward making Russia more E.V.-friendly began in 2022, when the government started subsidizing fast-charging stations and grid connections. In 2023, updated codes required E.V. infrastructure for new buildings. The number of public charging stations grew to more than 8,000 this year from fewer than 1,500 in 2022.

Fully electric vehicles have been exempted from the transport tax paid by owners of other vehicles in many Russian regions. In Moscow and other big cities, E.V. drivers do not have to pay parking fees, which can run as high as $9.50 an hour. Russian-made E.V.s are eligible for government subsidies and can use most toll highways free of charge nationwide.

Konstantin Alyabyev, the chief executive of Punkt E, Russia’s largest charging-station operator, said his company had recognized the potential of the country’s market early on.

“We don’t consider Russia to be some kind of cursed country,” he said. “The main blocker wasn’t any kind of natural barrier. There was the standard chicken-or-egg problem: When there were no electric vehicles, there was no infrastructure.”

In recent weeks, demand at Punkt E’s charging stations has doubled, with lines forming at some of them, Mr. Alyabyev said. But the company cannot quickly expand its network because of the time required to secure permits. Still, company officials decided to speed up the construction of 100 additional charging stations.

Mr. Tselikov, the auto expert, bought a sporty GWM Ora 03 GT. Previously, the model was known as the Ora Funky Cat. Mr. Tselikov nicknamed his own car Kotya, the Russian word for “kitty.”

He said that while the share of fully electric cars had doubled, they remained somewhat unusual in Russia, primarily because of their cost. Hybrid cars, he predicted, will continue to gain market share.

E.V.s may also face an image barrier in Russia. For some, they just are not manly enough.

Waiting in a long line for gas outside Moscow, Igor, 51, reflected that sentiment. “I would never buy an E.V.,” he said. “They’re bad for men’s health and way too expensive.”

Chico Harlan contributed reporting.

item.title: Spain’s Leader Calls Early Election After Housing Crisis Roils Government
item.description:
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of Spain called on Monday for an early election, days after his left-wing governing coalition, which lacks a majority in Parliament, lost a vote to pass a package of emergency housing measures.

The decision sets the stage for an election on Nov. 29, months ahead of schedule. Mr. Sánchez and his left-wing allies are seeking to frame it as an opportunity to resolve Spain’s housing crisis by ushering in a strong left-wing government.

The conservative Popular Party, which has topped recent opinion polls, and the far-right Vox party are focusing instead on issues like immigration, amid a crisis spurred by a surge of migrants this summer into Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa.

The vote is also set to be a referendum on Mr. Sánchez himself, one of Europe’s longest-serving leaders and a deeply unpopular figure among right-wing voters in Spain.

Mr. Sánchez has become a hero to the global left for standing up to the Trump administration over the war in Iran and for supporting renewable energy and inclusive immigration policies. At home, his popularity was dented by corruption accusations directed at his innermost circle, and, in July, by the sudden arrival in Ceuta of tens of thousands of migrants coming from Morocco.

The final straw was the defeat on Friday of housing measures that Mr. Sánchez had hoped would soothe public anger over rising evictions and soaring rents — symbolized by the recent eviction of María del Carmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman in Madrid. The loss showed that his governing coalition was essentially paralyzed and unable to pass key legislation.

But it also handed Mr. Sánchez an issue that could rally his left-wing base.

“To carry out the far-reaching reforms to reduce inequality,” Mr. Sánchez said in a press briefing on Monday, “we must mobilize to secure a much larger progressive majority in Parliament — one capable of taking on the elites, achieving new social advances and continuing to transform Spain.”

Mr. Sánchez said that voters would have to choose between keeping Spain as “a bastion of social justice” or “the far-right wave that brings regression wherever it governs.” That was a reference to Vox, which could join a right-wing government led by the Popular Party, the main conservative opposition group.

The Popular Party celebrated Mr. Sánchez’ announcement as a victory, as it had been calling for months for an early election. “Finally, the Spanish people will decide,” the party’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said on Monday.

“Housing is now out of reach, there are too few doctors and too many strikes, educational standards are declining — and immigration is out of control,” he added.

Santiago Abascal, the leader of Vox, said that his party was “ready” for a return to the polls.

“We’re going into an election with Ceuta invaded and with a candidate who is aligned with Morocco’s interests,” Mr. Abascal said in a TV interview on Monday, echoing a conspiracy theory that Mr. Sánchez is beholden to Morocco.

Recent polls have shown a rise in support for Vox. The party has placed third with around 18 percent in recent polls, while the Popular Party has been projected to win more than 30 percent. The Socialist Party is polling at around 26 percent.

But after eight years in power, Mr. Sánchez has built a reputation for political comebacks.

Pablo Simón, a political science professor at the Carlos III University of Madrid, said Mr. Sánchez was likely to campaign on the argument that a right-wing coalition would threaten social rights, including housing.

“That could mobilize some left-wing voters,” Mr. Simón said. Still, he added, a “renewed left-wing government” is “unlikely.”

Voters from both the left and the right welcomed the snap election.

Gonzalo Matías, a 28-year-old civil servant from Madrid, said he hoped the left would win a majority in Parliament. Mr. Matías called Mr. Sánchez “the best asset the left has” and praised his focus on human rights and social justice.

Chavela Quesada, an 82-year-old pensioner, said she believed the election was “the best news Spain could have received, because the country is sinking.” She called the current government “incompetent,” adding: “Everything they have done has been wrong: immigration, the invasion of Ceuta, everything is horrible.”

The early election added to recent shakiness in European financial markets. On Monday, the euro dropped to about $1.12, its lowest level since May 2025 against the U.S. dollar.

Despite the political turmoil, Spain is currently one of Europe’s economic bright spots. The country’s economy is expected to grow 2.1 percent this year, which is three times the rate forecast for the wider eurozone, according to Goldman Sachs.

While Mr. Sánchez has taken a tough approach to migrants illegally entering Spain from North Africa, his government’s relative openness to immigration from places like Latin America has supported economic growth. Spain’s unemployment rate is just below 10 percent, the lowest it has been since 2008.

Eshe Nelson contributed reporting from London and José Bautista from Madrid.

item.title: Are Babies Conscious?
item.description:
Andrea Edwards

Supported by

By pinpointing when it begins in young humans, scientists hope to better understand what consciousness is, and how it arises, in all of us.

By Carl Zimmer

Imagine that a scientist sits you in a device that can detect changes in the activity of your brain, and then plays a cycle of sounds. Over and over you hear three low tones, followed by a high one. Then you hear something different: four low tones in a row.

The scientist doesn’t have to ask you if you were aware of the change. That’s because our brains typically respond to an oddball sound with a brief, distinctive blip.

That blip turns out to be a surprisingly reliable marker of consciousness — that complex, mysterious state of being aware of one’s own thoughts and one’s existence in the world, which may also be present to some degree in other animals. People in a coma don’t produce this blip when they hear oddball sounds. Nor do people who are asleep.

Now imagine that the parents of a newborn bring their baby into the same lab for the same test. The tones play. Will there be a blip? Is that squirming, gurgling infant conscious? As humans, they are potentially conscious; we know that much. But in the moment, with their semi-developed brains and cognitive limitations — they can’t yet speak, focus their eyes, respond to instructions — they don’t seem to be conscious, at least not in the way adults are.Indeed, there’s an active scientific debate over whether newborns possess consciousness. Resolving it could help solve one of science’s most stubborn mysteries: what consciousness is, how it emerges and how we can know if another being possesses it.

Ask any researcher who studies consciousness, and they probably have a rough but useful definition. “Consciousness is a process of being receptive to the outside world and mixing that with our own internal world, to create the feeling of who we are and where we are,” said Dr. Topun Austin, a neonatologist at the University of Cambridge.

But Dr. Austin is well aware that this definition doesn’t speak to how that process plays out: where in the brain consciousness arises from the activity of neurons, or how their symphony of signals creates that feeling of being ourselves in the world.

Scientists have developed many detailed theories to address those questions. But there’s little accord on which is right, with no resolution in sight. “There’s not a consensus that we all agree on,” said Joel Frohlich, a cognitive neuroscientist at the University of Tübingen in Germany.

The stakes have only grown in recent years. Researchers have implanted millions of functional human brain cells in mice, for instance, prompting speculation that the work might someday endow mice with consciousness. Philosophers and theologians are musing about whether A.I. will become conscious, and how we can know for sure.

Amid all the uncertainty, there’s one fact that everyone can agree on. In each of our lives, there was a time when our brains were still too rudimentary to support consciousness, and there was a time when that changed. Even if we can’t say when babies gain consciousness, Dr. Austin said, “one thing we can be certain of is that they will become conscious.”

In recent years, Dr. Austin and other researchers have zeroed in on that transition. They are using new kinds of brain-scanning technology to study the brains of babies as never before, giving infants not only the blip tests, but even investigating what babies experience before birth. By determining when consciousness fully blooms, perhaps they can advance our understanding of how it works, and what it does, in all of us.

“I really see it as a frontier area in consciousness science,” Dr. Frohlich said.

When Charles Darwin became a father in 1839, he opened a notebook. Observing his children, he believed, could help him understand a question that fascinated him: “How does consciousness commence?”

By the time his first son, William, was born, Darwin had come to embrace the idea of evolution: The human mind, endowed with consciousness, had evolved over many generations from simpler instincts. Darwin also believed that all children followed a similar path in their early lives, as their brains developed from simple structures into complex vessels of thought. And so, starting with William and continuing with his subsequent children, he kept careful notes about how young humans changed over the first months of life.

At first Darwin recorded “instinctive actions” such as “sneezing, hickuping, yawning, stretching, and of course sucking and screaming.” Only when his children grew older did any mention of sophisticated behavior start to appear in his notebook: His children learned to recognize themselves in mirrors, spoke simple words, reached for objects. Before then, he declared, “There is no trace of consciousness in very young children.”.

Darwin was hardly an outlier in this belief. Doctors of the time also assumed babies were not conscious, and that assumption shaped their care of babies for generations. During surgery on newborns, for example, it was common not to use anesthesia; the drugs might damage a young brain — if babies weren’t conscious, what was the value of making them unconscious? As recently as the 1980s, doctors routinely withheld anesthesia from newborns, seeing no benefits that might offset the risks.

Doctors have since reversed this practice, as the study of babies has matured. More recent research has found, for instance, that newborns process pain signals in many regions of the brain, suggesting that their experience is similar to that of older children and adults.

Other studies have found signs that babies are capable of surprisingly complex forms of thought long before they can speak. They can recognize that a face is more than the sum of its parts; they can carry out simple forms of math in their heads. Findings like these made scientists rethink Darwin’s conclusion; perhaps consciousness emerges earlier than previously believed.

To explore that possibility, researchers have borrowed some of the methods used to gauge consciousness in adults, like playing those oddball sounds. In an experiment in Germany, scientists placed newborns in a special crib lined with sensors that could detect tiny magnetic fluctuations, then outfitted the babies with earphones. When the researchers played combinations of low and high tones, the brains of the babies produced distinct blips in response.

“It shows that the newborn brain is already performing very close to what we find in an adult brain,” said Claudia Passos-Ferreira, a philosopher at New York University.

But Dr. Passos-Ferreira and other researchers don’t consider that one finding conclusive. Some experiments have failed to find certain other markers of consciousness in babies. So researchers are running many different tests, to perhaps identify a cluster of markers of consciousness.

“If we see a lot of markers appearing at the same time, that’s highly suggestive that this is when consciousness begins,” Dr. Frohlich said.

Some of the most promising recent results have come from a major effort in London called the Developing Connectome Project. To carry it out, scientists had to modify a functional magnetic resonance imaging device. Normally, adult subjects lie on a table that slides into a large cylinder. Instead, engineers built a small cradle with a plastic head-cap at one end, to detect activity in a baby’s brain.

The project team ran brain scans on hundreds of babies, including newborns. They drew maps of the infant brains and recorded electrical activity that arose spontaneously during the 15-minute-long scans.

Lorina Naci, a neuroscientist at Trinity College Dublin, and her colleagues have been busy analyzing those recordings. One hallmark of consciousness in adults is the way different parts of the brain become active in a coordinated fashion. Those connections can evaporate when adults are asleep, or are under anesthesia. In recent studies, Dr. Naci’s team has discovered that regions of baby brains become active together in networks that are similar to those of waking adults, offering another early marker of consciousness.

In the meantime, new technology is speeding up data collection: Instead of putting babies in scanners, researchers can fit caps on their heads that monitor the brain with ultrasound or light.

As more markers of consciousness turn up in newborns, scientists have begun wondering what’s happening in the fetal brain, before birth.

Dr. Naci and her colleagues have found that some babies born prematurely also display networks of active brain regions that hint at conscious experiences. Dr. Frohlich and his colleague are studying fetuses that are still in utero, by having pregnant volunteers lean their bellies on a device that can detect the faint magnetic fields produced by fetal brains.

For now, consciousness before birth is an even bigger mystery than consciousness in newborns. Scientists generally agree that consciousness cannot emerge before the fetal brain has matured enough to receive signals from the senses, and then integrate them into a unified experience. Before about 26 weeks of gestation, those neural connections don’t exist.

How soon afterward these connections develop, scientists can only guess at. In a survey of experts by Dr. Passos-Ferreira, most estimated that infants have some consciousness by the time they are born.

“There are still some skeptics about infant consciousness who think that it emerges later,” Dr. Passos-Ferreira said. “It’s a minority, but they’re still there.”

As scientists map the birth of consciousness, they hope to gain a better understanding of how it evolved in humans in the first place. For children and adults, consciousness is vital for communicating through language, and for carrying out complex forms of thought. But if babies turn out to be conscious at birth, and long before they can talk or make plans for the future, then it must serve some additional purposes.

Perhaps, Dr. Naci said, consciousness allows babies to start making sense of the world as soon as they enter it, “to help them really hit the ground running in terms learning and development as soon they are born.”

But, she added, understanding consciousness in babies may demand a change in how we typically think of consciousness in general. By counting all the ways that the regions of a baby’s brain interact with each other from second to second, Dr. Naci and her colleagues have found that the baby brain actually exhibits more complexity than a waking adult’s.We tend to think of consciousness along a single line, on a gradient from unconscious to fully conscious. It’s the road we travel each day as we wake, and sleep. But what if consciousness has more dimensions, more ways of being?

Dr. Naci speculates that babies may be conscious at birth, but in a way that is perhaps more open to the world. “The idea is that they have this capacity to perceive more of the environment in much richer and more diverse ways,” she said. “They could have a very different experience than we have as grown adults.”

item.title: Saudi and Yemeni Forces Attack to Retake Control of Red Sea Coast
item.description:
Saudi Arabia and its allies in the Yemeni government attacked the Iranian-backed Houthi militia on Monday to try to reclaim territory along the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a choke point at the southern tip of the Red Sea.

The offensive was announced a day after the Yemeni government declared a full-blown war against the Houthis to retake territory it had lost to the militia over the past 12 years. The Yemeni government depends heavily on financial and military support from Saudi Arabia.

The offensive in Yemen has plunged the Middle East even deeper into conflict as the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran enters its eighth month with no end in sight.

A Yemeni military spokesman, Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili, announced the Bab al-Mandab campaign in a statement on social media. In a separate statement, a spokesman for a Saudi military coalition in Yemen, Maj. General Turki al-Maliki, said that 100 warplanes from the coalition were taking part in the a new operation called Yemen’s Dawn. That included airstrikes to support Yemeni government troops fighting in the Bab al-Mandab area, he said.

It was unclear whether any countries other than Saudi Arabia were participating in the air campaign.

The United States is providing military support to Saudi Arabia during the offensive, according to one current and one former U.S. official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matter.

item.title: British Museum Says It’s Extending Bayeux Tapestry Viewing Hours
item.description:
The British Museum may have expected about a million people to visit its landmark Bayeux Tapestry exhibition. But it is struggling to route all of the ticket holders through the space — despite limiting the text to read, having audio announcements urging people to move along, and even banning photography inside the gallery.

So on Monday, the museum said it was extending the exhibition’s opening hours, although it did not disclose what the new hours would be or exactly how they would align with the strict lighting and environmental exposure limits stipulated in the tapestry loan agreement with the French government.

A museum spokeswoman simply said in an emailed statement that it “has a careful plan for light hour allocations — agreed in partnership with colleagues in France.” The public response to the exhibition, the spokeswoman added, has been “extraordinary.”

The French Culture Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Given the long wait times for ticket holders, some of whom have reported standing in line for up to two hours to gain entry, the museum said it was taking that into consideration as it prepares to release the next allocation of tickets for the display, which runs through July 11.

The exhibition has faced logistical hurdles just weeks into its 10-month run as crowds gather to view the 220-foot-long embroidered cloth that depicts the events surrounding the 1066 Norman Conquest of England. It is the first time the tapestry, which has spent most of its life in France, has been displayed in England — where historians believe it was originally crafted.

Rocky, Reconsidered: The sculpture is at the center of a show by the Philadelphia Museum of Art that explores the meaning of monuments.

Route 66 Turns 100: Exhibitions recall the history of the neon corridor that helped define the American road trip.

A New Museum Comes With a D.J.: The space in Indianapolis, housed in a former dairy barn, aims to upend expectations of what an art museum can be.

The Fisher Collection in a New Light: A Bay Area family made a deal with SFMOMA that called for exhibitions of the collection’s works every 10 years.

More on Museums: Artists and institutions are adapting to changing times.

Before the tapestry’s arrival at the British Museum, there were concerns about the viability of transporting such a fragile textile. But an intricate plan was put together for its safe travel, and the British Museum has taken steps to conserve it during its time in London, including shutting off the gallery lighting at scheduled intervals to protect the tapestry from light degradation.

Now, the public is venting about other concerns including the wait times. A handful of ticket holders have been turned away because of the backlogs; the museum said those ticket holders had received refunds and priority booking slots for another time.

There was also scrutiny over accessibility. After Yusuf Ali Osman, a blind man from south London, filed a legal complaint accusing the museum of breaching the Equality Act 2010 by not providing audio-described tours for blind and partly sighted visitors, the museum announced that it was adding an “in-person audio-described tour.”

The museum also said on Monday that it would provide seating for visitors waiting in line.

The anticipation surrounding the display has been intense. When the first round of tickets went on sale in July, the museum said it had recorded its highest single-day ticket sales in history, generating more than 2.5 million pounds (about $3.4 million). King Charles III attended a private preview a week before the Sept. 10 public opening.

At the time, Mary Beard, the classicist and British Museum trustee, said that Britain had been swept up in “Bayeux fever,” in part because the tapestry depicts foundational national history.

This week, she told The Guardian: “We had to expect some teething troubles — this isn’t like an ordinary exhibition, everyone has come to see the same one object! The important thing is to put those teething troubles right.”

Described by the museum as “one of the wonders of the medieval world,” the artifact illustrates the events surrounding the Battle of Hastings — a date ingrained in British schoolchildren as the last successful foreign invasion of England and the origin of the modern monarchy.

Tickets are sold out through the end of the year, but additional batches are scheduled to be released this month and in January.

item.title: Former Prince Andrew Files Legal Action Against Police Over Warrants
item.description:
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly known as Prince Andrew, has begun legal action against the British police force that arrested him and searched his properties this year as part of its investigation into his links to Jeffrey Epstein.

Mr. Mountbatten-Windsor, the younger brother of King Charles III, was arrested in February on suspicion of misconduct in public office over accusations that he had shared confidential information with Mr. Epstein, the convicted sex offender. Mr. Mountbatten-Windsor was later released without charge.

Mr. Mountbatten-Windsor is challenging the legal status of search warrants that allowed the police to search two of his properties after his arrest, including his former residence at Royal Lodge in Windsor and another property on the king’s Sandringham Estate.

The search warrants were issued by the Old Bailey, England’s central criminal court, on Feb. 18, as part of the investigation, according to a statement from the British judicial office.

A private hearing in the case will be held on Thursday afternoon, the judicial office said.

The Thames Valley Police, the force that arrested Mr. Mountbatten-Windsor, said in a statement on Monday that it was “engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the Central Criminal Court.”

“As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further,” it added.

The police said that the investigation into the accusations of misconduct in public office was continuing. Mr. Mountbatten-Windsor has always denied any wrongdoing in his associations with Mr. Epstein, who died by suicide while in prison in 2019.

The depth of the two men's relationship was revealed in the Epstein files, the huge collection of documents, photographs and emails released by the U.S. Department of Justice this year, accelerating a decade-long fall from grace for the former prince.

Mr. Mountbatten-Windsor was stripped of his royal titles and kicked out of his longtime home, Royal Lodge, before his arrest on Feb. 19, his 66th birthday. It was the first time that a member of the British royal family had been arrested in modern history.

A photograph of Mr. Mountbatten-Windsor slumped in the back seat of a car as he left the police station that evening was splashed across the front page of many British newspapers the next day. One of the last British royal figures arrested before then was King Charles I, who was detained during the English Civil War in 1647, and who went on to challenge the lawfulness of those proceedings.

Since February, Mr. Mountbatten-Windsor has rarely been seen in public. In June, he was photographed leaving a horse event at the Sandringham Estate.

Some legal experts said that judicial reviews of this kind were not uncommon.

Andrew Gilmore, a partner at Grosvenor Law in London, said in a statement that because of the high-profile nature of the case, the warrants would have been thoroughly examined by the initial judge who issued them.

“Given the close public scrutiny this case has received, it would be very surprising if the police had not made every effort to ensure that the search warrants were properly obtained and lawful,” he added.Nick Vamos, a criminal lawyer at Peters & Peters and a former head of special crime at the Crown Prosecution Service, said that search warrants could be overturned on various grounds.

“However, even if the High Court ultimately quashes the warrants, that does not necessarily mean everything seized has to be returned or that the police can no longer use it,” Mr. Vamos said in a written statement.

The police can apply to the court to retain material if they have grounds to immediately seize evidence again, he explained, adding: “If there were more fundamental problems with the warrants, such as police acting in bad faith, they may be ordered to return all the material.”

item.title: How One Boeing 777 Exemplifies Iran’s Riskiness and Resilience
item.description:
The travelers speaking Persian at Ho Chi Minh City’s international airport last Monday dragged their bags toward an old Boeing 777 flying a new route — to and from Tehran. Many said they recognized it was a risky venture.

The plane, owned by Mahan Air, Iran’s largest private carrier, is one of just a few still defying a widened American effort to isolate Iran with threats to punish any entity that engages with its airlines. And because previous sanctions have barred suppliers from selling parts or services to Mahan for years, the dangers are also mechanical.

Iran’s aging aircraft — like the 23-year-old jetliner on the tarmac in southern Vietnam — are what sanctions experts often describe as “disasters waiting to happen.” Oman, Turkey and Iraq have stopped accepting Mahan’s flights. But not Vietnam, nor a few others. Recent stops for the 777 with tail sign EP-MTE also included Bangkok, Beijing and Moscow.

“Even if you don’t want to think about it, the danger is in your mind,” said Amir, 66, an Iranian in a golf shirt who was leaving Ho Chi Minh City, sharing only his first name to avoid trouble in Tehran. “Hopefully we’ll land safely. Hopefully nothing will happen.”

The story of Mahan Air’s old Boeing wide-body illustrates the risks that come with the Trump administration’s amplified campaign to make civil aviation a tool for coercion. In the aircraft’s travel record and reputation — pieced together with documents, tracking data and interviews with aviation and sanctions experts — there are warning lights aplenty.

Alongside the potential danger for civilians are hints of Iranian resilience and third-party resistance that suggest American threats can only go so far when so many still rely on energy from the Middle East.

Direct flights from Tehran to Vietnam only started in August, with plans to run weekly. Thailand added flights in July. The new routes appeared not long after Iran, in May, allowed several tankers heading for the region to pass through the Strait of Hormuz.

For the countries still receiving Iranian flights as of early October (along with China and Russia, the list includes Afghanistan, Armenia, Malaysia, Pakistan, Tajikistan, Thailand, Uzbekistan and Vietnam), the promise of future energy supplies appears to be a draw. And not just now. What if Iran keeps control of the Strait of Hormuz with tolls for adversaries, and expedited service for friends?

“That may be the trade off,” said Emanuele Ottolenghi, a senior fellow at the Center for the Research of Terror Financing who has studied Iran’s networks for decades. “Keep our flights open and we’re going to let your tankers travel.”

Some countries may also be trying to do a bit of superpower hedging.

The latest round of U.S. sanctions targeting companies that service, ticket or provide fuel to Iranian airlines threaten to exclude violators from the dollar-based financial system. China, a strong critic of that very system — and what it calls America’s “illegal unilateral sanctions” — has increased flights between Tehran and several cities, including Guangzhou, Shanghai and Beijing.

For countries determined to avoid the perception of alignment with either superpower, offering limited service to Iran lets them “more or less sit in the middle,” said Farzin Nadimi, a senior fellow with the Washington Institute for Near East Studies. “The new Mahan flights look like modest commercial and tourism links.”

Indeed, a dozen people in the airport check-in line said they had arrived with a packaged tour that delivered a week’s worth of beaches and sites across Vietnam. A few carried teal cone-shaped hats as souvenirs. Many described the trip as a way to convene with relatives coming from outside Iran and find respite from the grinding strain of life in a low-grade war.

But analysts doubted that tourism was, or will be, the plane’s only mission.

Mahan has been under sanctions from the U.S. Treasury Department since 2011 for alleged “dual use” violations that have included transporting weapons, military personnel, bulk cash and gold for the Iranian regime. Among Western intelligence agencies, it is known primarily as the airline run by and for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.

In April, EP-MTE was specifically identified and sanctioned by U.S. officials in a statement accusing Mahan Air of transporting unmanned drones around the world.

A few months later, President Trump updated executive orders aimed at terrorism with broader sanctions targeting Iranian aviation. The Treasury Department justified the measures by pointing to Mahan Air.

“Let this be a warning to anyone doing business with Iran’s remaining airlines, all of which we sanctioned today,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a September statement. “You are at risk of being cut off from the global financial system.”

The state-run company that operates Vietnam’s airports did not respond to requests for comment, nor did Vietnam’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Despite the American threats, EP-MTE is still flying.

Aviation records show it was one of five Boeing 777-200ERs delivered to Singapore Airlines between 2001 and 2003 that later moved to a Thai discount airline that went bankrupt during the pandemic. That led to nearly three years of storage in the Australian desert. Then, in 2023, a shell company registered in Florida, Ion Aviation, bought the planes and moved them to China, before another company, Udaan Aviation, registered the lot in Madagascar. Tracking data showed that the planes traveled from Cambodia to Iran in July 2025.

“This is a classic scheme that the Iranians have used for decades to acquire used aircraft, using an intermediary in some funny country,” Mr. Ottolenghi said. “They’ve used Armenia, Iraq, Malta and Madagascar.”

Such a large acquisition carried legal risks; 22 people in Madagascar were detained last year and accused of forging documents related to the transfers.

But safety is the lingering concern. Aviation enthusiasts have noted that for all five planes, the extended stay in an Australian boneyard most likely degraded fuel lines, rubber seals and metal engine covers. With the plane subject to an export ban, factory-certified reactivation — the industry standard after years of deep storage — did not occur.

Russian airlines, under sanctions since the country’s attack on Ukraine in 2022, have faced similar challenges. One company, S7, grounded its fleet of Airbus A320/1neo planes in 2024 for lack of maintenance.

“This highlights how sanctions on civil aviation can bite, but only slowly,” said Agathe Demarais, a senior policy fellow with the European Council on Foreign Relations. “Such sanctions are essentially a ticking time bomb for a country’s airlines.”

During the brief period when the nuclear deal that President Barack Obama had negotiated with Iran was in place, exemptions for aviation sales were granted, perhaps giving Iran a chance to stockpile vital components. Analysts said Iran could also be cannibalizing other planes for parts. Josefine Petrick, a policy fellow who focuses on the negative impacts of sanctions at the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation, a London think tank, called it “puzzle piecing a plane together.”

It can work, for a time. Flight trackers show that Monday’s flight landed safely in Tehran. But there is no denying the additional danger.

EP-MTE is one of at least two old 777s being used by Mahan to fly across Asia. The other is EP-MTB. Each one can hold more than 200 passengers. And with time, the mechanical risk compounds like interest, prompting complex questions about responsibility.

Who or what country or company would be blamed if one of Mahan’s 777s crashes?

“Sanctioning countries need to be aware and factor in the indirect effects of the policies that they push for,” Ms. Petrick said.

“Airplanes in Iran often operate twice as long as they would in other countries,” she added. “To some extent, these really are disasters waiting to happen.”

Tung Ngo contributed reporting from Hanoi.

item.title: Separatists Lead as Voters in Quebec Go to the Polls
item.description:
Voters in Quebec were preparing to cast ballots on Monday in a provincial election in which the separatist Parti Québécois appeared poised to gain power for the first time in more than a decade.

Polls showed the party could win a majority that would empower it to hold a referendum on Quebec’s independence in the next few years. The party’s leader, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, vowed to hold a referendum if the party wins, even though there is very low support for independence across the French-speaking province.

Increasingly confident toward the end of a 39-day campaign in which he focused mostly on other issues, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon exhorted voters to hand the party a majority of the 127 seats in the provincial legislature.

“I’m asking people listening to us to give us a real mandate that’s stable and strong over four years,’’ Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon said over the weekend in Quebec City. “A minority government makes it difficult to fulfill campaign commitments.’’

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon announced his plan for the first 100 days of a new government, saying that he would focus on lowering taxes, immigration levels and homelessness, as well as improving government efficiency.

By explicitly calling for a referendum during the campaign, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon broke with previous Parti Québécois leaders who opted for ambiguity to avoid alienating mainstream voters.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, 49, roused the party’s separatist base with his promise but spoke little about independence during the campaign itself. He also tamped down anxieties over a referendum by pledging to hold one only after President Trump leaves office and the economy stabilizes.

Voters displayed little interest in independence during the campaign, showing instead more concern over issues like the rising cost of living, the province’s dysfunctional public health care system, the lack of affordable housing and Canada’s trade war with the United States.

The Parti Québécois’s rivals seized on its promise of a referendum to portray Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon as a potential source of instability.

Christine Fréchette, Quebec’s premier and leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec, a center-right party that does not support independence and has been in power for the past eight years, said that a win by the separatist Parti Québécois would create economic uncertainty in Quebec, deterring investments in the province by both private businesses and the federal government.

While Mr. Plamondon has said he would not call a referendum before Mr. Trump leaves office, Ms. Fréchette said uncertainty will arise “the moment a referendum becomes part of Quebec’s political horizon.’’

She said, “That’s what’s going to happen Monday evening if people put the Parti Québécois in power.”

But Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has seemed able to overcome such attacks, benefiting from what polls described as Quebec voters’ intense desire for change. Ms. Fréchette took over as her party’s leader in April after the resignation of the deeply unpopular François Legault. But Ms. Fréchette, a former minister of economy, has been unable to distance herself from her party’s track record, especially the failure of several high-profile economic and government projects.

The Parti Québécois is also benefiting from an opposition split among four parties. Another major party, the federalist, pro-business Quebec Liberal Party, has been weakened by an abrupt change in leaders after an internal scandal. While the Quebec Liberals have held power in the past, including as recently as 2018, their support has shrunk in recent years to the multilingual, diverse electoral districts on the island of Montreal.

Polls have indicated that the Parti Québécois is strongest in rural regions of Quebec with strong concentrations of French Québécois voters. Historically, they have been the main supporters of the Quebec independence movement, including in unsuccessful referendums on sovereignty in 1980 and 1995.

Today, support for independence — around 30 percent — is at its lowest in decades. French Québécois are wealthier and better educated than in the past — and less interested in seceding from Canada, experts say.

As the attitudes of French Québécois have changed, and as immigration has risen in Quebec, many separatists have come to believe that the next referendum could be their last chance.

A majority government would allow Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon to initiate a referendum without seeking allies in other parties. Quebec’s other separatist party, Québec Solidaire — a left-leaning party popular among young voters — frames sovereignty differently. Rather than grounding independence in traditional French Québécois identity, it envisions an independent nation built on an inclusive coalition of all Québécois and the province’s 11 Indigenous groups.

Under Quebec’s winner-take-all electoral system, only one winner emerges in each of the province’s 127 electoral districts. Polls indicated that the Parti Québécois was close to securing at least 64 seats, which would give it a majority with only about 30 percent of the popular vote across Quebec.

item.title: Turkey Banned a Book by a Jailed Presidential Hopeful. We Read It.
item.description:
The book was being printed in late August, just days before its scheduled publication date in Turkey. Then the police showed up, stopped the presses and seized all copies, according to court documents.

The next day, a court officially banned the book, by a jailed opposition leader who had vowed to challenge President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Turkey’s next presidential election.

It never hit the shelves, meaning that very few people have read it. But The New York Times obtained a copy to try to understand why a work by one of Turkey’s best-known politicians was banned and what that says about the state of the country’s democracy.

The banning of the book, “The Nation is My Witness,” by the former Istanbul mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, came nearly two years into a crackdown that has seen scores of officials and members of Turkey’s political opposition arrested, mostly on corruption-related charges. Many remain in jail, and a number of mayors, including Mr. Imamoglu, have been removed from office.

In May, a court ousted the leadership of the Republican People’s Party, then Turkey’s largest opposition party, and reinstated its previous chairman, the man Mr. Erdogan defeated in Turkey’s 2023 presidential election. Many party members defected to a competing party, the New Party, dividing the opposition.

The government has barred critical social media accounts (including one that tracks blocked accounts). Last week, a court blocked the website and social media accounts of T24, an independent news outlet, deeming some of its coverage “L.G.B.T. propaganda.” (The outlet’s mobile app still works.)

Mr. Erdogan has been Turkey’s predominant politician for more than two decades, and his current terms ends in May 2028. But an early election is widely expected next year, which would allow him to seek another five-year term. He has not said whether he intends to run, but few doubt that he will.

It remains unclear who will represent the opposition.

Mr. Imamoglu faces an array of cases on charges including corruption, insulting public officials and espionage. He has denied all wrongdoing, and he and his supporters accuse Mr. Erdogan and his government of weaponizing the law to weaken their challengers.

“Do you know the real reason for the attempt to destroy the opposition?” Mr. Imamoglu wrote in his book. “It is to make the one-man regime permanent. The government knows this well: if there are fair elections, they will lose.”

Turkish officials insist that the country’s legal system is independent. Mr. Erdogan has portrayed the opposition as so corrupt that its illegal schemes extend like “the arms of an octopus.” Turkey’s Justice Ministry and the Turkish presidency’s Directorate of Communications did not respond to requests for comment.

Mr. Imamoglu’s book is a text version of the court defense he prepared — but never got to deliver — in a case accusing him of overseeing a criminal conspiracy inside Istanbul’s City Hall to enrich himself and fund his political ambitions. Prosecutors are seeking a prison sentence of more than 2,000 years.

Hoping to make his case directly to Turkish voters, Mr. Imamoglu found a publisher, who planned to print 22,000 copies and put them on sale on Aug. 30.

A few days before they went to market, prosecutors asked a court to block the book’s distribution, citing passages they said were “degrading and humiliating to the President, the judiciary, the government and public officials,” according to court documents.

On Aug. 27, the court banned the book “to ensure public order and prevent any crimes from being committed,” writing that the book’s content could increase tensions in society.

The Times’s reading of Mr. Imamoglu’s book found a work that feels like a long campaign speech — a political manifesto with a hint of legal defense.

While he praises supporters who protested in large numbers after his arrest, he makes no direct calls to action, instead urging people to vote and stand up for democracy and the Constitution.

His criticism of Mr. Erdogan and his government are unflinching, and he accuses them of abusing their authority to remain in power, endangering Turkish democracy.

“The issue is whether the ballot box you put in front of the people is real or fake,” he writes. “It is whether the elections are real or a sham, whether the multiparty system is real or a sham.”

Elsewhere, he accuses Mr. Erdogan of trying to “hollow out democracy and revoke, in practice, the authority of the nation to change the government.”

He addresses some of the legal charges against him, explaining, for example, why a method of municipal accounting his administration used was not corrupt. He also seeks to turn the accusations around, asserting that Mr. Erdogan is corrupt.

He offers a vision of what Turkey would be like with him in charge, including respect for democratic norms, more women in senior roles and greater judicial independence.

The book is not heavy on legal argument because Mr. Imamoglu views his prosecution as politically motivated, one of his former advisers, Serkan Ozcan, said in an interview.

“He said, ‘I’m an elected politician, I’m the mayor of Istanbul and I’m a presidential candidate, so my defense should be political,’” Mr. Ozcan said.

Mr. Ozcan called the book banning “a change of standards of democracy” driven by concern about Mr. Imamoglu’s political potential.

“It is Imamoglu they are afraid of,” he said. “They don’t want him to talk. They don’t want him to show himself. They don’t want him to do politics.”

Mr. Imamoglu was scheduled to present his defense in court in July, while NATO leaders were meeting in the Turkish capital, Ankara, drawing the news media’s attention elsewhere.

The judges allotted him less than two days to give his defense against an indictment that stretched to nearly 4,000 pages. Mr. Imamoglu objected and, after an argument, the chief judge ordered his removal from the courtroom and ruled that he had declined to offer a defense.

It remains unclear whether Mr. Imamoglu will find another publisher.

item.title: ‘No Help’: Aid Arrived Too Late as Ebola Spread in a Congolese Town
item.description:
On a hilltop town in eastern Congo, work has started on a new Ebola center. When completed, it will anchor an effort to contain the virus in the town and its surrounding villages.

Local health workers here say the center is too late.

Many lives could have been saved, the health workers say, had a sustained effort to combat the virus started in the town of Mangala in June.

In other towns in Ituri Province, the epicenter of the outbreak, Ebola treatment centers were set up weeks after the World Health Organization declared a health emergency in May. In Mangala, the Ebola response only started ramping up in August.

This outbreak, already the second largest on record, has reached seven different provinces in the Democratic Republic of Congo and likely began spreading as early as January. More than 3,900 people have died of Ebola in Congo since May, according to the latest data from the government.

There is tentative evidence to suggest that the response is making progress. The number of new cases reported each week appears to have reached a peak in August, according to recent figures from Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Outside aid organizations typically play a major role in African Ebola outbreaks, supplementing often weak government capacity.

But health workers in Mangala say fewer lives would have been lost had help arrived here sooner.

“There was no help, not even a bit,” said Godefroy Banzani, a senior nurse in Mangala, recalling how the town felt abandoned in the early weeks of the outbreak.

Experts say that what happened in Mangala underscores how this Ebola outbreak became the largest and fastest-growing that Congo has ever seen.

“With an epidemic, the slower the response, the bigger it grows,” said Julien Harneis, a senior Ebola response coordinator for the United Nations.

The current Ebola surge has surpassed total cases in the 2018 outbreak.

Source: Democratic Republic of Congo National Public Health Institute (data as of Sept. 29); United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs; World Health Organization.

Adina Renner/The New York Times

Health workers here offered several explanations as to why the response lagged in Mangala. One issue: the town has few hotels, forcing aid workers to make a three-hour trip each day from Bunia, the regional capital. The rutted road is so dusty that drivers sometimes have to stop because they cannot see, while after rains it can become too muddy to navigate.

Violent insurgents sometimes impose checkpoints along the dirt road leading into town. Foreign aid cuts have forced health workers to make painful choices about already scarce resources, including where to build Ebola centers, said Luca Fontana, a senior W.H.O. official with years of experience fighting the virus.

Privately, however, some international health workers said that Mangala was simply overlooked. Dr. Wessam Mankoula, head of emergencies at Africa C.D.C., acknowledged the concern in Mangala and said that it was difficult to establish treatment centers in every health zone affected by the virus.

When the W.H.O. declared an outbreak in mid-May, there were already hundreds of Ebola cases in Ituri Province, setting the overall response on the back foot from the start. But health teams in towns such as Mongbwalu, Bunia and Nizi, were quickly mobilized to educate communities on infection.

As those efforts were underway, Mangala remained on its own, officials here say.

When The New York Times visited the town in September, signs of the struggle to contain the virus were everywhere. The coming treatment center, which will be run by the international humanitarian medical charity Alima, was just a patch of flattened red earth.

In the meantime, Mangala relies on the district hospital, where in the early months of the outbreak, Ebola patients were treated in a mud house with no windows, an earthen floor and little ventilation.

One afternoon in September, health workers set fire to their protective clothing after use, sending dark smoke skyward as the synthetic material burst into flames.

The fire burned yards from an area accessible to villagers.

Most treatment centers in Ituri Province are strictly divided into green and red zones. Patients and suspected Ebola cases are kept in the red zone, and anyone entering must wear protective clothing. In the separate green zone, medical staff members and visitors can enter safely, talking with patients at a distance or through plastic screens.

But at the regional hospital in Mangala, staff members said people with signs of the virus circulated freely across a central, grassy courtyard.

Mave Liripa, 26, came to the hospital with her mother and 1-year-old daughter, Justine Ngabusi, in September. All three showed signs of Ebola, including fever and vomiting, Ms. Liripa said.

Ms. Liripa’s 8-year-old son had died with Ebola symptoms the previous week, and the family buried him at home, she said.

Nurses wearing protective gear took blood samples from the family to be sent for testing. Nurses told the family to sit on a bench, which was near patients with unrelated illnesses.

“Everywhere is a red zone here,” said Dr. Jacques Savo Bamuhiga, the medical director in Mangala. Five nurses and a doctor have contracted Ebola at the hospital already, and one nurse has died, Dr. Bamuhiga said.

The government stopped paying Mangala’s hospital staff at the start of the crisis. It gave no reason for the suspension, but the decision damaged morale and hindered efforts to organize a response, doctors said.

Some heath workers quit, while others staged a brief strike. Though they have since returned to work, some said that they had still not received their salaries. Dr. Bamuhiga praised the staff who had worked unpaid through the crisis.

Congo’s health minister, Roger Kamba, acknowledged that some health workers had not been paid. The government was working to resolve the problem quickly and would add a bonus to health worker salaries, he said.

Hospital treatment increases the chances of patient recovery, which helps to convince residents of the benefits of disclosing to medical workers when someone is ill. Ebola patients are most infectious in the final days of the illness and just after death, making safe burials essential.

All this reduces community transmission. But people must first be persuaded to allow sick relatives to be treated in hospitals rather than at home.

In Mangala, a fledgling outreach team was only established in August. As a result, fears spread unchecked through the town that the hospital was injecting its patients with Ebola, staff members said.

Residents boycotted the hospital and, even as late as early September, treatment rooms that were usually packed with patients before the outbreak, remained empty.

On top of the elevated community transmission caused by home treatment and unsafe burials, more people have died of conditions unrelated to the virus because they were too afraid to go to the hospital, Dr. Bamuhiga said.

A single ambulance was recently assigned to the Ebola response team in Mangala and nearby villages, but several residents said they have sometimes waited days for its arrival.

The ambulance, a four-wheel drive, picked up six patients on a recent afternoon. The patients scrambled into the car’s bench seats. Nurses had no choice but to cram three suspected Ebola patients next to patients with unrelated illnesses.

How many people could have been saved in Mangala had help arrived sooner is difficult to determine. Dr. Bamuhiga put the official Ebola death toll in the town at 165, but said that number failed to reflect the many deaths at home.

At least 200 people have died in nine villages near Mangala, said Josephat Pilo Mandje, a government representative in the area.

The fate of Bonheur Njabu, 22, reflects that of many others.

When he fell ill with Ebola symptoms, he initially kept it secret, according to his mother, Jeanne Ngawey. When he finally told her he was sick, she hurried to the village, but no ambulance was available to take him to the hospital. Motorbike taxis refused to take him, fearing infection, she said.

The only drugs Ms. Ngawey could get were from a tiny local pharmacy. Despite her efforts, her son died, she said. One day later, a team of health workers laid him to rest in the town’s red earth. Dozens of people gathered at the gravesite, singing hymns and wailing.

Among the mourners was the president of the local youth council, Olivier Alike, 25. He had witnessed the outbreak as it tore through Mangala.

“I would like everything to go back to how it was before,” he said.

item.title: In a Major Boost for the Right, Another Bolsonaro Nears Brazil’s Presidency
item.description:
A surprise victory for a right-wing populist embroiled in scandal. Crushing defeat for a party deemed out of touch with its base. Supporters on the left grasping for answers.

The scene may feel familiar to Americans. This time, it unfolded in a Latin American nation thousands of miles away. And the results could profoundly reshape the region and its relations with Washington.

Brazil’s right-wing challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, didn’t win the presidency Sunday night, but seemed well on his way to victory.

His surprisingly strong showing gives a significant boost to the ascendant right in Latin America, placing Brazil, the region’s most populous country, within reach as the biggest electoral prize following seven straight wins by right-wing candidates.

It also represents a remarkable comeback for the Bolsonaro family four years after Mr. Bolsonaro’s father tried to subvert democracy after losing the last election, was convicted of plotting a coup and sentenced to prison.

Flávio Bolsonaro himself overcame being embroiled in a corruption scandal to win more votes than the leftist incumbent, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. While neither clinched enough ballots to win in the first round of voting, Mr. Bolsonaro’s formidable performance appeared to foreshadow a win in a two-way contest on Oct. 25.

That is because the votes of some 9 million Brazilians who backed various minor right-wing candidates on Sunday will now be up for grabs. The vast majority are likely to shift their support to Mr. Bolsonaro, giving him the upper hand. For Mr. Lula, finding more votes presents a far more challenging task.

The regional swing to the right is driven by an array of forces, experts say, including dissatisfaction with incumbent governments, deepening worries about security and crime and a shift toward more conservative values.

For months, polls had predicted a close race between the two men, with Mr. Lula leading by the slimmest of margins. The leftist president had framed his candidacy as the only way to halt the return of the Bolsonaro family to power, just four years after Jair Bolsonaro lost the last election and inspired his supporters to storm the capital, demanding that the result be overturned.

Mr. Lula had also sought to portray his candidacy as defending Brazil’s sovereignty against attempts by the Trump administration to intervene in the country’s domestic affairs.

Mr. Bolsonaro had struggled to shake off a corruption investigation and divided voters with his plans to seek amnesty for his father and the rioters. Then, on Sunday, he surprised many when he captured 47 percent of the vote, finishing two points ahead of his rival.

“Even Jair Bolsonaro may be surprised by this result,” said Jairo Nicolau, a prominent political scientist and professor at the Getúlio Vargas Foundation, a research institution.

A runoff win for Mr. Bolsonaro would represent a major triumph for President Trump, ejecting Mr. Lula, one of his most outspoken foes among world leaders, who has not shied away from challenging the American leader.

It would also usher in an enthusiastic ally willing to help Mr. Trump’s bold plans for dominance in the region.

It is not yet clear just what brought Mr. Bolsonaro to the brink of victory.

“It was conceivable that Flávio could come close to Lula or even overtake him,” said Mr. Nicolau. “But what happened in Brazil was a right-wing tidal wave,” he added. “We’re going to spend a long time trying to understand.”

What unfolded in Brazil may have echoed a broader challenge incumbents face across the region: convincing voters to give them more time to deliver on pledges.

“Basically, it’s never a good thing to be president in South America,” said Guilherme Casarões, professor of Brazilian studies at Florida International University in Miami. Governments on the left and the right have struggled to win second consecutive terms across the region.

Some analysts believed Mr. Bolsonaro had managed to rally at least a slice of conservative voters planning to vote for other right-wing contenders. Disillusionment with Mr. Lula’s party, which has been in power for the better part of two decades, also most likely fueled his challenger’s success. Many Brazilians are concerned over pervasive violence and crushing personal debt.

Mr. Bolsonaro has tried to link his rival to a corruption scandal sweeping Brazil’s Supreme Court. The Brazilian president has tried to distance himself and called for judicial overhaul.

The momentum of the Brazilian right was also on full display in the nation’s legislative races, where right-wing candidates, including four other members of the Bolsonaro family, made spectacular strides in both Congress and the Senate.

“A complete takeover of the far right,” said Mr. Casarões.

This means that, whomever ultimately wins the presidency, Latin America’s largest democracy is poised to keep marching to the right — a prospect that excited Carlos Augusto Marques, a 63-year-old writer casting a vote in Rio de Janeiro.

“To improve, we need four or five center-right governments, at least,” he said.

If Mr. Bolsonaro wins, his party’s gains could allow him to deliver some of his most polarizing promises: an amnesty for his father, pardons for participants of the Jan. 8 riots and a Senate more willing to try to remove justices who convicted his father.

Now, the presidential contest is headed for what is likely to be a bitterly contested final leg, with both candidates racing to capture millions of more votes. Yet the pathway to victory may prove far more daunting for Mr. Lula.

Analysts say he could still stage a comeback, particularly if he could win over some of the 33 million Brazilians who skipped Sunday’s vote.

In Brazil, voting is mandatory for most people between the ages of 18 and 70, though absentees only face a small fine. This year, the number of Brazilians who sat out the first round rose to a record high of 21 percent.

Mr. Lula may also succeed in striking coalitions with other parties in hopes of convincing some moderate voters who reject Mr. Bolsonaro to shift their support to him.

Alberto Saab, 55, is among the eight percent of voters on Sunday who supported a third-party candidate. The engineer has voted for both candidates in the past, but remains undecided so far for the runoff.

He has been impressed with leftist investment in education, yet he also supports the right’s bolder measures to combat security. “The world is very polarized,” he said. “If we don’t return to some sort of center of balance, I think we’ll remain in a difficult situation.”

Mr. Bolsonaro is being investigated for raising millions for a biopic about his jailed father from a disgraced banker at the center of a massive fraud. Details of the probe have dominated public debate, fueling expectations for more bombshell revelations closer to the final vote.

In recent weeks, Mr. Lula has seized the opportunity to dial up attacks on his rival’s record. His campaign aired an online minidoc exploring controversies in Mr. Bolsonaro’s political career and a video linking Mr. Bolsonaro’s alleged ties to militias. Some voters may not be swayed in either direction. Kailhany Machado, 23, voted for a third candidate and plans to cast a blank ballot in the runoff.

“Flávio is involved in several scandals and Lula? I don’t even need to tell you,” Ms. Machado said. “They’re corrupt, criminal, and don’t deserve our vote.”

Mr. Trump has been a wildcard in Brazil’s presidential race.

Ahead of the runoff, he could stay quiet, openly endorse Mr. Bolsonaro or ratchet up pressure with new measures aimed at Brazil.

Last year, Mr. Trump stepped in to help Mr. Bolsonaro’s father avoid a prison term. Nevertheless, the elder Mr. Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years in prison, though he is serving his term at home because of poor health.

Mr. Trump has not championed any presidential candidate, though his administration has appeared to lift Mr. Bolsonaro in more subtle ways ahead of the vote. This has alarmed Brazil, which has accused the United States of trying to sway its elections and has put up a firewall to try to shield its democracy from threats.

Flávio Bolsonaro has aligned himself with Mr. Trump and other right-wing leaders in the region, echoing plans to mount a hard-line attack on the drug gangs that have become a major concern for many ordinary Brazilians.

And, like Mr. Trump, Mr. Bolsonaro is now looking to rewrite his own nation’s history.

Isabela Cruz and Leonardo Coelho contributed reporting from Rio de Janeiro. Seth Kugelcontributed reporting from São Paulo. Thayz Guimarãesand Alice Macielcontributed reporting from Brasília.
