item.title: Why Saudi Arabia’s Last War in Yemen Turned Into a Quagmire
item.description:
The government of Yemen, backed by Saudi warplanes, launched an offensive on Monday to try to retake the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a day after announcing a major military campaign against the Iranian-backed Houthi militia.

The new campaign has evoked memories of the last time Saudi Arabia intervened against the Houthis in Yemen.

In March 2015, the Saudis launched an air campaign in the country and led a coalition of mostly Sunni Arab states, most notably the United Arab Emirates.

The stated goal was to restore the Yemeni government that the Houthis drove out of the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. But despite years of fighting, that did not happen, and a brutal war helped cause one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

In 2022, a fragile truce was agreed and most of the fighting abated. But the agreement began to unravel in July this year, after the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing the airport in Sanaa. The truce collapsed last month when a sweeping Houthi military offensive took over Yemen’s Red Sea coast.

Here is what happened in 2015 and how it’s connected to the new round of the conflict.

In March 2015, Saudi Arabia announced the formation of a 10-country military coalition and the launch of a bombing campaign against the Houthis to try to restore the government. But the campaign was effectively a two-country effort, with Saudis and Emiratis doing most of the fighting and committing the most resources.

For Saudi officials, the threat felt existential. Saudi leaders said they feared that a hostile force on their southern border would function as a proxy for Iran, the kingdom’s main regional adversary. Tehran provided the Houthis with weapons and training, but many analysts say its initial role was modest and that the Houthis are a distinct, homegrown movement driven primarily by domestic and regional ambitions.

The war also carried a political dimension: Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler, was 29 at the time and had recently been named defense minister. The intervention in Yemen was his first major act.

The Emirates had its own agenda. Its leaders viewed Islah, the Islamist-leaning party at the heart of the anti-Houthi coalition, with profound distrust. By cultivating proxy forces in Yemen, the Emirates sought control over key maritime commercial hubs along the country’s southern coast, analysts said. These connections included the Southern Transitional Council, an armed political group with ambitions to create an independent state that directly undermined the authority of the Yemeni government it publicly supported.

When the Saudi-led coalition recaptured Aden in 2015, that appeared to presage a broader Houthi defeat. But the effort to extend the offensive stalled and the militia fortified its positions near Sanaa, locking front lines in place for years as the Saudi-led air campaign dragged on. Coalition aircraft repeatedly struck civilian infrastructure but were unable to neutralize the Houthis or destroy their weapons stockpiles.

The anti-Houthi alliance also fractured: Rival Yemeni groups opposed each other and growing friction between Saudi Arabia and the Emirates caused problems, too.

An Emirati-led offensive to seize the Red Sea port of Hudaydah in 2018 descended into stalemate. The coalition was eventually forced to pull back under international pressure as Yemen teetered on the brink of famine.

In August 2019, the Southern Transitional Council turned its weapons on its Saudi-backed allies and seized control of Aden, the interim capital of the government that the coalition had sought to restore. The Emirates began drawing down its forces in Yemen, and a power-sharing deal was agreed in November to integrate the separatists into the Saudi-backed government. But instead of unifying the coalition’s factions, this resulted in even deeper splits as each group sought to protect its own interests.

The United Nations has said that the war helped caused one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, contributing to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people from violence, hunger and disease.

The coalition was accused of war crimes after airstrikes hit crowded markets, wedding halls, hospitals and funeral gatherings. Houthi forces were accused of indiscriminate artillery shelling, of deploying land mines in populated areas, and of systematically recruiting child soldiers.

The coalition enforced air and maritime blockades around Yemen, maintaining that such measures were vital to intercept Iranian weapons shipments. Hudaydah, which handled about 70 percent of Yemen’s food and medical imports, suffered years of bombings. But humanitarian agencies said the restrictions harmed the civilian population, pushing many toward starvation and helping to cause one of the worst cholera epidemics in modern times.

Beyond the billions spent on the war, the military campaign eroded Saudi Arabia’s international reputation and exposed the kingdom to Houthi drone and ballistic missile strikes.

The war also became a political liability for Prince Mohammed, and severely strained relations with Washington. The U.S. Congress repeatedly voted to limit American military aid because of the human toll of the war.

The Houthis have not been defeated. The group still controls Sanaa and much of Yemen’s populous northern highlands and it has become a more formidable military force, equipped with long-range missiles and attack drones.

item.title: A Bolsonaro Win Would Nearly Complete Trump’s Latin America Map
item.description:
Right-wing candidates in Latin America have won the last seven presidential elections since the start of 2025. Number eight — Brazil — might be weeks away.

The right’s winning streak is a major boost for President Trump’s desire to have ideologically-minded allies to partner with as he seeks to impose greater U.S. control over Latin America.

On Sunday, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of Brazil’s former hard-right president Jair Bolsonaro, received the most votes in the election’s first round, making him a strong favorite for the presidency when he faces off against President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva later this month.

For the right, Brazil, Latin America’s largest nation and economy, would be the biggest prize.

Brazilians also gave right-wing politicians control of Congress and governorships across the nation, including four new federal lawmakers with the last name Bolsonaro. (They are the former president’s wife, two other sons and brother.)

In a larger context, the results are not that surprising.

Politics in Latin America have long swung back and forth.

Just a few years ago, left-wing candidates were on a winning streak, claiming countries like Brazil and Colombia and giving them control over most of the region.

And a pendulum always swings back. But this lurch to the right in Latin America — in Colombia, Chile, Honduras, Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador and Costa Rica — is coming at a particularly consequential moment.

The Trump administration is bent on exerting new levels of control over the region with tariffs, sanctions, airstrikes, visa revocations, election interventions, an oil blockade on Cuba and the capture of Venezuela’s leader.

It’s President Trump’s more aggressive version of the Monroe Doctrine, the 1823 claim of U.S. primacy in Latin America. And the pairing of Mr. Trump’s policy with the right’s ascendance is creating a fundamental shift in the region, particularly when it comes to security.

The Trump administration has made its top priority in Latin America a new war on drugs. The administration has compared fighting the region’s powerful cartels to the war on terror in the Middle East, and has acted accordingly.

The State Department has labeled 21 criminal groups in Latin America as terrorist organizations. The Pentagon has carried out 71 strikes on boats in the waters around Latin America, killing nearly 240 people it claimed were drug traffickers. (Many legal experts consider the strikes illegal.) And last month, American soldiers joined a police operation in Ecuador against a cartel.

That is the sort of cooperation the Trump administration wants to expand. Eighteen Latin American nations have joined a new U.S.-led coalition against cartels, and at least four of them — Colombia, Guatemala, Honduras and Ecuador — have already agreed to joint military operations with the Pentagon.

Brazil — with its 200 million citizens spread across a country that accounts for roughly half of South America’s size — has been the biggest missing piece. But that will change if Mr. Bolsonaro wins the runoff on Oct. 25.

Mr. Bolsonaro has been an eager Trump supporter for years, as his father was one of Mr. Trump’s top allies during his first administration. Mr. Bolsonaro has already said he would add Brazil to the anti-cartel coalition, called the Shield of the Americas, and work with the United States to fight Brazilian gangs.

He had suggested in social media posts last year that he would welcome U.S. military intervention in Brazil, though he denied that in recent interviews, saying the cooperation would be limited to intelligence. But it was Mr. Bolsonaro who successfully lobbied Mr. Trump to designate two Brazilian gangs as terrorist groups.

It’s not the first time the U.S. and Latin America have tried to fight drug gangs together. But the degree of ideological alignment across the region, as well as the Trump administration’s willingness to intervene militarily, has made this an exceptional moment.

Security experts say the coordination could aid intelligence, especially in tracking criminal financial networks — which have long been a problem for Latin America.

In August, the Pentagon announced a new task force for the Western Hemisphere designed to act as a hub for intelligence and operations among allied countries. And last month, 14 nations followed Washington’s lead and designated various cartels as terrorist organizations.

The largest cartels are effectively multinational corporations, trafficking drugs and laundering money across borders, and so the designations could enable governments to better attack their finances with sanctions.

“You were on your own,” Mr. Trump told his Latin American allies at the United Nations last month. “You’re not on your own anymore.”

At the same time, the Trump administration has signaled that it’s less eager to help leftist governments. That was the case in Colombia before voters there elected Abelardo De La Espriella, a lawyer who has vowed to take an especially hard-line approach to cartels. And as part of a larger diplomatic tiff with Mr. Lula’s leftist government in Brazil, the White House has withheld visas for federal police agents from the country.

Mexico, the other big Latin American democracy still run by a leftist government, has actually expanded its security cooperation with the administration, but the U.S.-Mexico relationship is unique in the region. (Uruguay, whose population is 3.5 million, is the third leftist democracy left in the region.)

There are still questions about whether the counter-cartel coalition can make a difference. Experts say the Pentagon’s boat strikes have hardly slowed the flow of cocaine. And there are few specifics on how countries will actually work together, and what becomes of the effort once Trump is out of power.

There are also questions on what it means for Latin America's citizens and sovereignty. The imbalance in political, economic and military power between the United States and any one Latin American nation is significant, even with Brazil.

Mr. Trump, for instance, tried to intervene in the criminal case against Mr. Bolsonaro’s father, who faced charges for attempting a coup, by imposing 50 percent tariffs on Brazilian products. That effort failed and Jair Bolsonaro was convicted, but Mr. Lula has warned since that Latin America must retain its ability to govern itself in the face of pressure from Washington.

Mr. Bolsonaro, however, has argued that the threat to sovereignty comes not from Mr. Trump but from the cartels. To fight them in Brazil, Mr. Bolsonaro has promised to learn from Nayib Bukele, the president of El Salvador whose authoritarian tactics has drastically lowered crime rates while also drawing complaints of human rights abuses.

In his nation of six million, Mr. Bukele has locked up tens of thousands of young men with little due process, placing many in what he calls “mega-prisons.” Mr. Bolsonaro, who said he has studied Mr. Bukele’s approach, has proposed building five similar prisons, and has also called for lowering the age of criminal responsibility to 16 and chemically castrating rapists and child abusers.

Latin American leaders have increasingly spoken highly of Mr. Bukele’s approach and the results it has yielded, making El Salvador one of the region’s safest nations. Mr. Bukele, who has called himself the world’s coolest dictator, is also, according to polls, one of the world’s most popular presidents.

item.title: Russia Moves to Tamp Down Speculation About Plague in Siberia
item.description:
The rumors have been swirling for days. That a young lab worker died of suspected plague in Siberia. That the authorities feared an epidemic might spread and had quarantined hundreds of people.

While concrete information is scant, conflicting reports abound. The name of the lab worker. Her age. If she died or what she may have died from.

Russia’s consumer watchdog, which oversees disease control, has said only that “an employee of an anti-plague institute in the Irkutsk Region” was “diagnosed with pneumonia” of unknown origin.

That has not stopped the rumors — fueled in part by contradictory statements from local officials as well as by a widespread distrust of the Russian authorities, who have in the past concealed emergencies, like the AIDS outbreak in the 1980s — from making international headlines.

With the Kremlin on Monday urging people to ignore speculation, here is what to know.

The Russian consumer watchdog did not name the employee. In a statement carried by state news outlets and published in pieces, the agency said that “no microorganisms linked to her professional activity were identified in the patient’s samples” and that “no health changes related to infectious pathology” had been identified among her contacts.

A commission also checked the anti-plague institute in Irkutsk for compliance with “biological safety requirements,” the agency said, and “no emergency situations involving pathogenic microorganisms were identified.”

The Irkutsk institute conducts research on a number of infectious diseases, including plague, which is caused by a bacterium. While there are a few hundred cases globally every year, mainly in Africa, plague can be easily treated with antibiotics if caught early.

In its statement, the consumer watchdog added that the “sanitary and epidemiological situation” in the Irkutsk region was “stable.”

The statement was issued on Sunday, two days after initial reports emerged about something more concerning happening in the Irkutsk region, which is about 2,600 miles east of Moscow.

The first signs of a potential issue came on Friday, when the Irkutsk regional governor said that he had held “an extraordinary meeting” with Russia’s chief sanitary physician about “a suspected case of a particularly dangerous infection in a resident.”

“All identified contacts” of the resident “have been placed under medical observation,” the governor, Igor I. Kobzev, wrote in a statement on social media.

That day, the mayor of Shelekhov, a town close to the city of Irkutsk, the regional capital, said that he had received “many inquiries” from residents and could confirm that the local hospital’s inpatient department was closed for quarantine. The mayor, Maksim N. Modin, said the hospital’s laboratory had suspended operations. He urged residents “not to spread rumors.”

The governor of the neighboring Buryatia region, Aleksei Tsydenov, was the first to officially raise the prospect of plague. He said on Friday that “the woman who died of plague in the Irkutsk region” had not visited Buryatia. His post on a state-linked messaging app was later updated to read “possibly died of plague.”

The following day, the authorities in Baikalsk, a town about 50 miles from the city of Irkutsk, cited “unofficial information” about “a case of plague” in a statement advising against travel to Shelekhov. That statement, on Telegram, was later deleted.

So were at least three posts by Ren-TV, a federal news network, including one that named the deceased lab worker and reported that she had researched plague.

Mr. Modin, the Shelekhov mayor, said on Monday that the consumer watchdog had the situation “under strict control,” adding, “a set of anti-epidemic measures is being carried out.”

Local news media have painted a bleaker picture. Lyudi Baikala, a regional outlet, reported that in addition to the Shelekhov hospital, other clinics and a maternity ward had been closed in Irkutsk.

Pavel Stepanov, a local journalist, posted on his Telegram channel that a young laboratory assistant had broken a test vial and died. That statement could not be independently verified. In a subsequent post on Monday, Mr. Stepanov defended his reporting and questioned why some government agencies and Kremlin-friendly news outlets had deleted statements and stories about Irkutsk.

The authorities, he said, “should investigate whether all this is not a sabotage by our enemies, who are acting with increasingly sophisticated methods.”

Officials in the United States and the European Union have said they are aware of and monitoring the reports about Irkutsk.

A potential lab leak and a feared disease prompted some comparisons with Covid-19, but experts noted that even if plague were confirmed, the risk would be limited. Human cases of plague occur each year and are relatively simple to treat.

Professor Ian Jones, a virologist at the University of Reading, England, said in an emailed statement that the Irkutsk case “seems like a rare lab accident and is unlikely to go much further.”

This is a developing story and we still don’t know many details. Together with several colleagues we are trying to figure out what really happened in Irkutsk. What questions would you like answered? What do you think we should delve into? You can also submit confidential tips here: https://www.nytimes.com/tips

Oleg Matsnev, Michael Mason and Koba Ryckewaert contributed reporting.
